newsitem.title: ZAIRE: ZAIRE OPPOSITION TRIES TO OUST KENGO AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: ZAIRE OPPOSITION TRIES TO OUST KENGO AGAIN.

text.p: Zaire's opposition banded together in parliament in a fresh attempt to oust Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, winning a vote on the floor of the house and promising to follow it up with street protests.

But supporters of Kengo and ailing President Mobutu Sese, most of whom boycotted Tuesday's session, said that the vote fell far short of the three-quarters majority needed under Zaire's transitional constitution to sack the prime minister.
"You need three quarters of the signatures of parliament and today there were not even half of the members present," Anzuluni Bembe, a Mobutu supporter and parliamentary vice-president, told Reuters.
Kengo is in Kenya for talks on the crisis in Central Africa. Mobutu, who has spent most of his time in Europe since prostate cancer surgery there in August, is in hospital in Monaco.
The radical opposition led by Etienne Tshisekedi sponsored the motion, which called for a ceasefire and peace talks with rebels in the east.
Opposition spokesmen said as many as 462 of the assembly 738 members took part in the debate. A majority of those present approved the motion by acclamation.

Opposition militants said that the vote was valid and that students would demonstrate on Wednesday in support of it. The Kengo government has banned all street protests for the duration of the war in the east.
Opposition supporters advanced parliamentary technicalities in support of their demand that Kengo must go.
"We reached three-quarters in comparative terms, in formal terms and the vote was higher than when Kengo was elected," Augustin Kipukama of the radical Lumumbist movement told Reuters.
Tshisekedi, leader of Zaire's main political opposition, is a veteran opponent of Mobutu.
A national conference elected him prime minister in 1992 but Mobutu sacked him a year later.
The transitional parliament elected Kengo in 1994 as a compromise candidate -- a move Tshiekedi and his followers have always bitterly contested.
Tshisekedi and his Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) enjoy widespread support among Kinshasa's poor and urge peace talks with the rebels.
"We should avoid taking decisions that violate the constitution," said Kanga Boongo, one of the few Mobutu supporters who stayed for the debate.
Witnesses said some dissident Mobutu supporters voted with the opposition.
Earlier, assembly members spent five hours debating what the debate should be about.
